grammar: Saying what something is with です
sentence: 私は学生です。
hiragana: わたしは がくせいです
meaning: I am a student.
description:
X は Y です is the sentence for saying what something is: a name, a job, a home country. です is the polite “is / am / are,” and one form fits every subject. \


## The Topic Marker は “wa”
The は after X is the topic marker, the small word that flags X as what the sentence is about. Each sentence then names one fact about that topic. Notice the order: the topic comes first and です closes the thought. The topic can be anything that a speaker wants to talk about (It can be an object, location or any other grammatical element). The topic marker ”wa” roughly corresponds to English ‘as for’. The topic particle while written as 「は」, is pronounced 「わ」.


## だ / です (da / desu)
**だ** statements are directed at the speaker rather than the listener and serve to communicate self-expression. They are used to convey emotions, among other things. On the other hand, **です** is used to direct a statement at a listener, showing the speaker's awareness of them.


## Making it negative
To say X is not Y, keep X は and change the ending. In conversation じゃないです is the everyday choice, じゃありません is the textbook standard, and ではありません is the formal, written-sounding one. All three are fully polite, so pick by how formal the moment feels.

description:
でした is the past of です: it turns “X is Y” into “X was Y.” For the negative, じゃありませんでした does the same job for “was not.”

Use でした when a noun sentence or a な-adjective sentence is about the past: yesterday's weather, last week's plans, what someone used to be. Do not use it after an い-adjective (a describing word that ends in い, such as 寒い); those build their own past, 寒かったです.

The negative has two polite forms. じゃありませんでした is the formal one; じゃなかったです is lighter and more common in speech. Both are polite, so pick by how formal the moment feels.

grammar: Asking questions with か and question words
sentence: あなたは学生ですか。
hiragana: あなたは がくせいですか。
meaning: Are you a student?
description:
We often think of particle か as "the Japanese question mark," but it's actually a marker of the unknown. It can be used to mark a sentence as a question, or to express alternatives, like "either … or …" in English. 

Take any plain statement, put か on the very end, and you have a yes-or-no question. Nothing else moves: the subject, the object, and the verb all stay where they were. In writing か already marks the question, so a question mark is optional.


## Question Words
For anything beyond yes or no, use a question word. It sits exactly where the answer would sit, so you do not pull it to the front. 

何 (nani): What
誰 (dare): Who
どこ (doko): Where
いつ (itsu): When
どんな (donna): What kind of
どの (dono): Which (of several)
いくら (ikura): How much

grammar: これ・それ・あれ: Whose Space the Thing Is In
sentence: これは私のかばんです。
hiragana: これは わたしの かばんです。
meaning: This is my bag.
description:
これ, それ, あれ, and どれ are a set of こそあど words. You can use them to refer to things (specific objects that are physically present) you want to talk about, without specifying what they are. They are the equivalent of "this one," "that one," and "that one over there" in English.

Most languages split “this and that” into two words, and Japanese splits it into three. The choice follows whose space the thing is in: yours, the listener's, or neither. これ points to something in your own space, それ to something in the listener's, and あれ to something outside both. Do not choose by distance alone: それ marks the listener's space even when that person stands beside you. 


## The question word is どれ, “which one.”
どれ is used to ask "Which one?" or "Which ones?" However, どれ can only be used when asking about a choice of three or more people or things. When you only have a choice of two options, you'll use どっち (or its polite version どちら) instead.

description:
Japanese sorts pointing words three ways: near me, near you, and away from us both.

こ・そ・あ・ど + れ / こ / の

| Distance        | Thing (alone) | Place (alone) | + noun |
|-----------------|---------------|---------------|--------|
| Near me (こ)    | これ          | ここ          | この   |
| Near you (そ)   | それ          | そこ          | その   |
| Over there (あ) | あれ          | あそこ        | あの   |
| Which? (ど)     | どれ          | どこ          | どの   |


## Question word:
**どの** (followed by noun) can only be used when asking "which…?" out of a choice of three or more people or things. When you only have a choice of two options, you'll use どっち (or its polite version どちら) with the particle の instead, as in どっちのドア (which door?)

**どこ** is the question word that pairs together with these characters, and asks "where?"

description:
Japanese uses two different verbs to say that something exists. あります is used for things that do not move on their own, and plants belong here too. います is used for anything that moves under its own power: people, animals, and insects.

がある (ga aru): there is (used for non-living things)
がいる (ga iru): there is (used for living things)

Use these two verbs to say what is in a place, and mark the place with に. 
**place + に + thing + が + あります / います**


## Negatives and having
For the negative, あります becomes ありません and います becomes いません. The same two verbs also say that you have something: 時間があります means “I have time,” and 兄がいます means “I have an older brother.” What you own is treated as something that exists, so the same rule still picks the verb.

grammar: How Counters Work
sentence: 写真を三枚撮りました。
hiragana: しゃしんを さんまい とりました。
meaning: I took three photos.
description:
Most languages count with a number and a noun: three pencils. Japanese adds a third word — a counter — that changes with the shape or kind of thing you count.

### N を + number + counter + verb

Pick the counter from the object's shape: 枚 for flat things, 本 for long thin things, 匹 for small animals, 人 for people. When you are unsure, the all-purpose つ works for most objects up to ten. Do not put the bare number straight in front of the noun: it sits after を, right before the verb.

| counter |hiragana  |usage|
|--|--|--|
|枚 | まい | for flat things |
|本| ほん | for long things|
|匹|ひき|for small animals |
|人|にん|for people|
|つ|つ|all purposes/general|


## The sound changes
Counters that begin with an h-sound, like 本, shift after certain numbers. After 1, 6, 8, and 10 a small っ appears and ほ hardens to ぽ: いっぽん, ろっぽん, はっぽん, じゅっぽん. After 3 it softens to ぼ, giving さんぼん.

The other numbers stay plain: にほん, よんほん, ごほん, ななほん, きゅうほん.

grammar: The topic marker は, and も for “also”
sentence: あの人も日本人です。
hiragana: あのひとも にほんじんです。
meaning: That person is also Japanese.
description:
## The Topic Marker は “wa”
The は after X is the topic marker, the small word that flags X as what the sentence is about. Each sentence then names one fact about that topic. Notice the order: the topic comes first and です closes the thought. The topic can be anything that a speaker wants to talk about (It can be an object, location or any other grammatical element). The topic marker ”wa” roughly corresponds to English ‘as for’. The topic particle while written as 「は」, is pronounced 「わ」.

## Adding to a group with も "mo"
も fills the very slot that は or が would take, and it marks its word as one more of a group already in play. Once you have said that one person is a bank clerk, swap は for も to add the next person.

The particle も is similar to the English words "too" and "also." It is placed after a word to show that the word is part of a set. To conceptualize the particle も, it's helpful to imagine a list on a memo (me-も) sheet. The list is a group of things or people that belong together. When も goes after a word, it indicates that the word is a member of the group.

も often follows a noun or a noun phrase. What comes after も can be a lot of varieties of words and forms. It can be anything from nouns, い-adjectives, な-adjectives, to verbs in either the positive or negative form.

grammar: は vs が: choosing your subject marker
sentence: 猫がいます。
hiragana: ねこが います。
meaning: There is a cat.
words: 猫|が|います
description:
The particle が goes after a noun to show us that the noun is the subject of a sentence. That is, the noun before が is the person or thing that's doing whatever comes next. In other words, が marks the grammatical subject. 

Use が when the subject is new to the listener: something that appears, or a question word like who. Use は when you both already know the thing and you are saying more about it. One rule to keep: a question that asks with が is answered with が — do not switch to は.

|Situation|は  or  が|Example|
|--|--|--|
|Something new appears in front of you|が|あ、車**が**来ました。|
|You name a topic already known|は|あの車**は**部長のです。|
|A question word is the subject|が|どちら**が**山田さんですか。|
|You answer that question|が|わたし**が**山田です。|

Beyond marking the subject, が also puts emphasis onto that subject, and excludes other possible subjects.

description:
の can express ownership or possession when it comes after a person or a group of people. This is the use that is similar to …'s in English. You put your name on your things, right? Labelling is important for showing ownership!

You might think of particle の like Japanese equivalent of the possessive 's ending in English, as in Tom's car of Granny's kittens. However, the label maker is really a better way to think of particle の, since the relationship between the label and the noun can result in various different interpretations. 

It can be express ownership: わたしのかん
or that something belongs in a particular group: 会社の人
or is a type of something: 日本語の本

の joins nouns only: when the describing part is a verb or an adjective, a different pattern takes over.

grammar: Saying Where Things Are: に and Position Words
sentence: 机の上に本があります。
hiragana: つくえの うえに ほんが あります。
meaning: There is a book on the desk.
words: 机|の|上|に|本|が|あります
description:
Particle に is a complex particle with many uses. Some linguists have found that it can be used in more than twenty different ways! However, if you boil に down all the way to its basics, you'll find that it has a fundamental meaning that unites all its uses. In short, に shows you where something is, was, or will be in the future. It's used to pin down something, whether it's location, time, purpose, or condition.

In this section, we're going to learn に to pin the place where something or someone exists: the spot where you find it. For finer location, a position word joins the noun with の, as in 机の上に, “on the desk.” Use に with ある, いる, and 住む “to live,” where the point is that something is there. Do not use it for the place of an action: that place takes で.

## Finer Position
Fine location sits between the noun and に: **noun + の + position word. **

| Position word | Meaning | In use |
|--|--|--|
|上(うえ)|On / above|机の上に|
|下(した)|Under / below|いすの下に|
|中(なか)|Inside|かばんの中に|
|前(まえ)|In front of|店の前に|
|うしろ|Behind|家のうしろ|
|となり|Next to|コンビニのとなりに|
|近く (ちかく)|Near / nearby|駅の近くに|

description:
Particle で appears in a lot of different contexts, and is an important particle to wrap your mind around. Its meaning shifts depending on how it's used, but, at its core, particle で helps specify where or how an activity or an event takes place. 

で marks the place where an action happens, and に marks where something exists or arrives. One picture decides it: if you can see someone doing something there, the spot takes で.

に points to a place as a state: where you are, where you live, where you arrive. で points to the place where you do something. Do not use で for existing or arriving: いる, ある, 住む, and 着く all take に.

grammar: Marking Where You're Headed with に and へ
sentence: 駅へ歩きます。
hiragana: えきへ あるきます。
meaning: I walk to the station.
words: 駅|へ|歩きます
description:
Both に and へ attach to a place to mark where you are headed. With a movement verb such as 行く, 来る, or 帰る, either one is correct. These two are particles — the small words that mark a word's job in the sentence. に treats the place as the endpoint you reach, and へ treats it as the direction you move toward.

## Difference between に and へ
Particle へ is like an arrow, pointing the way to the destination. Particle に on the other hand, does not indicate a path at all, it just acts like a pin on a map, marking your final destination.

The sense of directionality that particle へ carries makes it more significantly different from に in other contexts. If you use a verb that expresses movement, but lacks a sense of direction, then particle へ can help add direction

コンビニへ歩いた vs コンビニに向かって歩いた

The particle へ indicates a destination, or the direction that something is heading. It's written with the hiragana character へ /he/, but this is always pronounced like the え /e/ character when it's used as a particle.

### へ For Physical Destinations and Directions
へ marks destinations, while also highlighting the route someone (or something) takes to get there. Thus, particle へ is often followed by a verb that expresses directional movement. For example, verbs like 行く (go) and 来る (come).

### へ For Figurative Destinations and Directions
You can also use へ to mark a figurative destination or direction. Such as goal or objective.

### へ For Recipients
へ is also used to indicate the recipient of something.

description:
The particle と wears a lot of hats, but its fundamental meaning is quite simple — to connect two or more things together as companions.

と and や both join nouns into a list, but they promise different things. と says the list is complete; や gives a few examples and leaves room for more. Use と when you can name every item, and や when you are only giving a sample. Do not put と after the last item, and do not close a と list with など (“and so on”); など belongs with や.

**N と N / N や N (など)**

## A different と: with, not and
One more と looks the same but marks the person you do something with: 友だちと行きます is “go with a friend.” The test is what と joins. Two things of the same kind in one slot make a list; a person marked with と is your companion.

hiragana: しちじに おきます。

description:
Particle に is a complex particle with many uses. Some linguists have found that it can be used in more than twenty different ways! However, if you boil に down all the way to its basics, you'll find that it has a fundamental meaning that unites all its uses. In short, に shows you where something is, was, or will be in the future. It's used to pin down something, whether it's location, time, purpose, or condition.

In this section, we'll learn about when to use it for time words.

Japanese marks a **fixed point** in time with に and leaves relative time words bare. Clock times, weekdays, dates, and months take it, while 今日 and 毎日 never do. Use に for a time that names a slot on a clock or a calendar. Do not use it with a word that points at now, because 今日 and 毎日 shift as the day moves.

**fixed time word + に + verb**

grammar: から ・まで:  Where a Range Begins and Ends
sentence: 朝から夜まで働きます。
hiragana: あさから よるまで はたらきます。
meaning: I work from morning until night.
words: 朝|から|夜|まで|働きます
description:
から marks where a range begins and まで marks where it ends. The same pair works for stretches of time and for distances between places.

**から** is a particle that marks the **source**, such as a starting point, an origin, or a reason.

**まで** is a particle that indicates the **end** point in space, time, and numbers. In its most basic use, it marks an end point of a connection between two points, such as with a distance or over a period of time.

Use から and まで for any span with two edges: opening hours, a break, a route, a work week. The earlier edge takes から and the later edge takes まで, never the other way around. For a deadline, not a stretch, Japanese uses までに instead.

から is the equivalent of English “from,” and まで does the work of both “to” and “until.” Each one can also stand alone when only one edge matters. あしたから means “starting tomorrow,” and ここまで means “this far and no further.”

grammar: Going Somewhere to Do Something: Verb Stem + に + 行く
sentence: 本を買いに行きます。
hiragana: ほんを かいに いきます。
meaning: I go to buy a book.
description:
Japanese builds “go somewhere to do something” as one compact phrase. Take the verb stem, add に, then finish with a verb of motion.

Use this pattern whenever a trip has a purpose: going to buy, coming to meet, returning to fetch. Do not close it with an ordinary verb, because the last slot needs motion: at this level 行く, 来る, and 帰る.

**V-stem + に + いく / くる / かえる**

Start from the ます form, drop the ます, and the stem is what remains. Attach に and a verb of motion, so 買います “buy” gives 買いに行きます “go to buy.” A noun that names an activity fills the same slot on its own: 買い物に行きます “go shopping.”

When you name the place as well, the order is fixed. The destination with に or へ comes first, then the object with を, then the purpose, then the motion verb. That gives デパートへ靴を買いに行きますデパートへくつをかいにいきます “go to the department store to buy shoes.”

sentence: 朝起きて、顔を洗います。
hiragana: あさ おきて、かおを あらいます。
meaning: I wake up in the morning and wash my face.
description:
The て form is the all-purpose connecting shape of a verb. One conversion gives you requests (てください), permission (てもいい), the progressive (ています, an action going on now), and joined actions.

How you build the て form depends on which of the three verb groups a verb belongs to. Ru-verbs and the two irregulars swap the ending for て directly, and u-verbs take one of six endings. In polite speech the て form is a connector, not an ending, and on its own it is only a casual request like 待って (wait).

Read the table by group. For ru-verbs and the irregulars, the rule is a single swap, so only the two irregular forms need memorizing.

sentence: ここに名前を書いてください。
hiragana: ここに なまえを かいて ください。
meaning: Please write your name here.
description:
Add ください to a verb's て-form (the connecting form: 撮る becomes 撮って) and you have a polite request. It reuses the ください of をください, but here you ask for an action instead of an object.

Use てください to ask someone for an action, in a store, a classroom, or a taxi. Do not use it alone with a boss or a customer, because it can sound like an order. Open with すみませんが or switch to くださいませんか instead.

## Asking for an object vs. an action
One question settles the choice: are you asking for a thing, or for an action? をください asks for an object, and てください asks for an action.

てください|Please do X|A request or instruction
てくださいませんか|Would you please do X?|A softer, more polite request

Put each action into its て form and keep the real order of events. The final verb alone shows whether the chain is past or present, polite or plain. Change that one ending and the whole chain follows.

description:
ています has three jobs: an action going on now, a state that stays after a change, and a habit. English -ing matches only the first, so the other two are where learners slip.

**V-て + います**

Use ています whenever English would ask what someone is doing, or what their life looks like these days. Do not use it for a one-time future plan: 東京に住みます announces a move, while 住んでいます describes the life you already lead.

## 1. In progress
The first job is the true be -ing: the action has started and has not finished. Here the English map holds cleanly.
## 2. A state that stays
When a verb names a one-moment change — 結婚する, 住む, 持つ — ています describes the condition left behind. 結婚しています means someone is married now, not that a wedding is under way.
## 3. A habit
A repeated routine also takes ています. A time word such as 毎朝 or 週に二回 is usually the clue.

description:
もう says an action is already done, and まだ says it is still going. Both flip meaning when the verb turns negative: “no longer” and “not yet.”

##  もう
At its most basic, もう means "already" and もう〜ない means "not…anymore." 

もう expresses something relative to the existing amount or state of things. And, "already" and "not…anymore" are relative expressions that are always based on a certain point in time. As its core, もう signifies that you have a certain reference point in mind and what you're talking about has already passed the point, or will not pass that point anymore.

##
まだ is a versatile adverb that can be used to express something you're still in the process of doing, or something you haven't done yet. Used in a positive context, まだ means "still," whereas in a negative context, as in まだ〜ない, it implies that something has "not yet" happened.

At its core, まだ has similar connotations to the English "yet" – it assumes a pre-determined baseline for comparison, or reference point, by which the topic of a まだ statement is measured. To put it simply, まだ expresses that whatever it is you're talking about hasn't passed that point of reference, yet.

もう + past|Already done|もう食べました
まだ + positive|Still, continuing|まだあります
もう + negative|No longer|もうありません
まだ + negative|Not yet|まだ出していません

description:
Japanese compares two things with two markers, each with its own job: より marks the standard, のほうが marks the one you pick. Which noun comes first does not change the meaning.

**A + より + B + のほうが + adjective**

Use this pattern when you weigh two named things against each other: two drinks, two routes, two seasons. のほうが marks the one you choose, and より marks the thing you compare it with. Do not use it for the best of a whole group, because that is the job of 一番.

## Asking which one you prefer
To ask which of two things someone prefers, list both with と and end the question with どちらが. The answer names your pick and adds のほうが, and the noun the question already supplied can be omitted.

description:
一番 in front of an adjective makes it the most or the best. The group you compare within takes で, as in 日本で.

The order is fixed: range, then the subject with が, then 一番, then the adjective. The adjective never changes shape, so 高い stays 高い and 好き stays 好き. Do not add より “than”: 一番 already means “the most,” and the two together double up.

The range is usually marked with plain で, as in 日本で or 一年で. When the group is a set you belong to, add 中 first: 家族の中で. To ask which one wins, put a question word plus が in front of 一番, and the answer echoes that が.

## Patterns:
A の中で B が一番〜です → Of A, B is the most ~
A で B が一番〜です → Among A, B is the most ~
どれ／どの + N が一番〜ですか → Which is the most ~?
一番 + adjective → the most ~ / the best
